about: Every table the apps' code once carried, by <File>.<name>: categories, labels, aliases, route lists, colors (#hex), lookup tables, tuples as rows of cells, structs as objects. Edit a value and the apps pick it up on their next refresh; remove a key and the app's own table returns. Keys come from scripts/merge_app_keys.py (the Mac exports them from the code). MyBlock.sources (builds from 115): extra NYC Open Data sources for Home's block card, each an object {id, dataset, kind (event|film|closure|permit|filing), where (SoQL with {BORO} {Boro} {BOROCODE} {LIKE} {TODAY} {UNTIL} {SINCE30} {BLOCK} {BBL}), select, street/from/to (field names) or location (one field holding 'STREET between A and B'), start, end, title and detail (templates with {field}), group (fields that make one row)}. MyBlock.sourcesOff: names of built-in sources to switch off: sapo, film, filmdata, closures, permits, filings. MyBlock.buttons (builds from 117): the pills under the block card's next 30 days, each {title, dest, when}; dest is feeds (311, crime and permits on the address), web:<site path>, screen:<route key> or dk:<DK route>; when is cb6 or always. MyBlock.hide: rows of the block card to leave out: offblock (the 'more on <street>, off your block' list), filings, map. MyBlock.hide also takes "ballot" (builds from 117): the Home block card's sample ballot row, the block's ballot26 lines from the blocks file, stays off the card. MyBlock.rows (builds from 117): the Home block card's rows, in order, each {id, title, icon (SF symbol), color (#hex)}; ids trash, parking, polls, precinct, subway, reps, ballot, park, nearby, or "field:<key>" for any field of the block's data in the blocks file (zones, hist, school, sector, ballot29, hn, built...). Drop a row to hide it; add one to show it. Rows can also be {"id": "button", "title", "dest" (feeds | card | web:<site path> | dk:<route> | screen:<key> | https://...), "color"}, {"id": "text", "title", "text" or "key" (text.json)} and {"id": "web", "page": "<site path>", "height"}, each at its spot in the list, so a button or a page of the site can sit between any two rows of the card. Site pages in the app (home.json "web" sections, tools "screen:web:<path>") take {ADDRESS} {LAT} {LON} {SLUG} {CD} {BBL} {NUMBER} in the path, filled from the saved address, and get window.__bkcbPlace. HomeStatus.tiles (builds from 120): the day's strip on Home, in order, {"id": today|parking|sanitation|schools|subway|weather, "dest"}; a tile with a dest is a button to that screen key, web:<site path>, dk:<route> or https link; leave a tile out to drop it. The subway and weather tiles open the Weather screen, where the MTA service card lists the lines' delays and changes. <File>.ds.<id> (builds from 121): every NYC Open Data dataset a screen reads, by its id; put another dataset id there and that screen reads it instead. HomeStatus.sanitationUpdate: a link for the day's strip; on days without collection the Sanitation tile opens it.

BidsOrgsView.sections.title: The steps
steps: Local property owners, merchants and civic groups form a steering committee and work with the Department of Small Business Services to write a district plan: the boundaries, the services, the budget, and the formula for how the assessment is calculated.
The district plan goes first to the City Planning Commission, which forwards a copy to the City Council and to the affected community board within five days.
The community board notifies the public, may hold a public hearing, and may submit a written recommendation to the City Planning Commission within 30 days of receiving the plan.

The Commission reviews the plan and the recommendations, holds a public hearing, and prepares a report. It sends that report to the Mayor, the borough president, the City Council and the affected council members, with copies of any community board recommendation, within 60 days of the close of the board's review period.
The City Council votes a local law establishing the district. The Mayor signs it. That local law is what brings the BID into existence.

BidsOrgsView.sections.title: Who runs it once it exists
BidsOrgsView.sections.body: Day to day operations belong to a district management association, a nonprofit board. Under the Administrative Code, a majority of that board must represent property owners, and tenants of both commercial space and dwelling units must be represented as well. Four more seats are appointed: one each by the Mayor, the Comptroller, the borough president, and the council member representing the district. When a BID spans more than one council district, that fourth appointment is made by the Speaker of the City Council after consulting the council members involved.

BidsOrgsView.sections.title: Who pays
BidsOrgsView.sections.body: The assessment is levied on property inside the district, billed and collected by the city, and then passed through to the BID, which delivers the services. Many commercial leases let a landlord pass the assessment on to the tenant.

BidsOrgsView.sections.title: What has to go back to the Council
BidsOrgsView.sections.body: Amending a district plan, expanding boundaries, or raising an assessment all require returning to the City Council. A BID is not a one-time decision. It is a standing relationship between a commercial corridor and city government.

ExploreViews.types: Flagship Park
A large destination park serving the whole borough or city, with major facilities and dedicated administration. Prospect Park is CB6's flagship.
Community Park
A mid-size park serving several surrounding neighborhoods, typically with a mix of active and passive recreation.
Neighborhood Park
A smaller park serving the immediate area around it, usually within walking distance of the people who use it.
Playground
A property built around play equipment, typically with safety surfacing, sprinklers, and seating.
Jointly Operated Playground
A playground on Department of Education property, run jointly by NYC Parks and the school. Schools use it during school hours and the public uses it after.
Recreational Field/Courts
A property made up primarily of ball fields or courts rather than general parkland.
Garden
A community garden or planted green space, often licensed through the GreenThumb program.
Triangle/Plaza
A small paved or planted space, usually formed where streets intersect at an angle.
Strip
A narrow band of parkland, often running along a roadway, median, or waterfront edge.
Undeveloped
Mapped parkland that has not been built out for public use.

NYCHAView.codes.text: Referrals from city agencies, including families with children referred by Homeless Services, households displaced by fire or vacate order and referred by HPD, and referrals from HASA and ACS.
Certified victims of domestic violence, and intimidated witnesses referred by a District Attorney’s office.
Substandard conditions or rent hardship: homeless, involuntarily displaced, doubled up or overcrowded, or paying more than half of gross household income in rent.
No need based preference, or households that neither live nor work in New York City.
Applicant is already the lessee or co-lessee of a public housing or Section 8 apartment.

Working family priorities, banded by share of area median income. W3 is up to 30 percent, W2 is 31 to 50 percent, W1 is 51 to 80 percent. W0 covers working families with children referred by Homeless Services.

NYCHAView.eligibility: The applicant or co-applicant is 18 or older, or an emancipated minor.
At least one member of the household is a United States citizen or has eligible immigration status.
NYCHA’s definition of family covers two or more people related by blood, marriage, domestic partnership, adoption, guardianship or court awarded custody, and also covers a single person living alone.
Household income is at or under the limits below.
Senior buildings have their own rule: the head of household, or head and co-head, must be at least 62, and every other permanent member must be 62 or older.

NYCHAView.steps.title: File the application online
NYCHAView.steps.text: Applications go through ApplyNYCHA on the Self-Service Portal at selfserve.nycha.info. You do not attach any documents at this stage.

NYCHAView.steps.title: Answer what it asks
NYCHAView.steps.text: Total household income, who is in the household, your current living situation, and a first and second borough choice.

NYCHAView.steps.title: Watch for the letter
NYCHAView.steps.text: NYCHA sends a letter within 30 days of submission. You can also check status any time on the Self-Service Portal.

NYCHAView.steps.title: Renew every two years
NYCHAView.steps.text: An application stays active for two years. Use “Update/Renew My Case” on the portal before it lapses and you keep your original filing date.

NYCHAView.steps.title: The eligibility interview
NYCHAView.steps.text: This is where NYCHA verifies everything you reported. Applicants are called in based on priority code and how long the certified application has been waiting.

ReviewProcessView.elurpStages.label: DCP certifies
ReviewProcessView.elurpStages.tip: Certified by the Department of City Planning. The clock starts here.

ReviewProcessView.elurpStages.label: Community Board and Borough President
ReviewProcessView.elurpStages.tip: Community Board and Borough President, 60 days combined: under ELURP the CB and Borough President review runs in one shared window. CB6's recommendation is still advisory. The project must meet the affordability threshold.

ReviewProcessView.elurpStages.label: City Planning Commission
ReviewProcessView.elurpStages.tip: City Planning Commission, 30 days: streamlined review. On the Council track the Council then has 30 days for the final vote.

ReviewProcessView.findings: A
Unique Physical Conditions
The property has an unusual physical feature, like an odd shape, steep slope or below-grade lot, that is specific to this site and not shared by neighboring properties.
There are unique physical conditions, such as irregular shape, topography, sub-surface or size, that create practical difficulties in complying with zoning.
B
No Reasonable Return Without Relief
Because of those unique conditions, the owner cannot make any reasonable economic use of the property under current zoning. Not just less profitable: unusable as of right.
Because of those conditions, there is no reasonable possibility of developing, rehabilitating or using the property in strict conformity with zoning without substantial financial hardship.
C
Variance Is the Minimum Necessary
The relief being asked for is the smallest deviation from the zoning rules that would fix the problem. The applicant cannot ask for more than they need.
The requested variance is the minimum necessary to afford relief. The applicant must show the variance does not exceed what is strictly necessary.
D
No Harm to the Neighborhood
Granting the variance will not hurt the surrounding neighborhood: it will not set a bad precedent, block light and air, or damage nearby property values or character.
Granting the variance will not alter the essential character of the neighborhood, impair the use or development of adjacent properties, or be detrimental to the public welfare.
E
Not a Self-Created Hardship
The hardship was not created by the current owner. You cannot buy a property knowing it has a zoning problem, then ask the BSA to fix it for you.
The practical difficulties or unnecessary hardship claimed were not created by the owner or a predecessor in title.

ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.label: Classify the action
ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.tip: Is the action Type I (more likely significant), Unlisted (case by case) or Type II (exempt)? Type II actions need no further review.

ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.label: Lead agency
ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.tip: When several agencies are involved, one is designated lead. The lead agency coordinates the full environmental review.

ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.label: EAF review
ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.tip: Environmental Assessment Form: the applicant completes Part 1. The lead agency completes Parts 2 and 3 to assess significance.

ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.label: SEQR determination
ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.note: Neg Dec, CND or Pos Dec
ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.tip: The lead agency issues one of three findings: Negative Declaration (no significant impact), Conditioned Negative Declaration (impacts manageable with conditions) or Positive Declaration (significant impact, an EIS is required).

ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.label: EIS if needed
ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.tip: Required only on a Positive Declaration. The draft EIS is scoped, prepared and released for public comment, and a final EIS is issued before any agency decision.

ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.label: Findings statement
ReviewProcessView.seqrStages.tip: After the final EIS, the lead agency issues a Findings Statement weighing environmental impact against social and economic factors before making a decision.

ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.label: DCP certifies
ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.tip: Certified by the Department of City Planning. Every deadline below runs from this date.

ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.label: Community Board
ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.tip: Community Board, 60 days: CB6 holds a public hearing and issues an advisory recommendation. This is CB6's moment in the formal record. The vote is not binding but carries real weight.

ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.label: Borough President
ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.tip: Borough President, 30 days: issues an advisory recommendation. Like CB6, not binding, but the CPC and Council pay attention.

ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.label: City Planning Commission
ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.tip: City Planning Commission, 60 days: holds a public hearing and issues the first binding vote. Can approve, modify or disapprove. If modified, the City Council gets a 15-day CPC scope review.

ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.label: City Council
ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.tip: City Council, 50 days: the second and final binding vote. Council members representing the affected district have enormous influence. Can approve, modify or disapprove.

ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.label: Mayor
ReviewProcessView.ulurpStages.tip: Mayor, 5 days: can veto the Council's decision. The Council can override with a two-thirds vote within 10 days.
